newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-G10 monitoring fx markets closely - Tietmeyer.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-G10 monitoring fx markets closely - Tietmeyer.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said on Monday that the Group of 10 (G10) industrial nations would continue to monitor foreign exchange markets closely, but avoided commenting on the recent strength of the dollar.

Tietmeyer said a meeting of central bank governors from the G10 nations had been briefed about the situation on the gold and foreign exchange markets, but he declined to give details of their discussions.
"We will monitor further developments on foreign exchange markets very, very closely," he said after chairing the monthly meeting of the G10 governors at the Bank for International Settlements.
The dollar has surged to five-year highs against the mark recently, supported by a strong U.S. economy and speculation about a Federal Reserve credit tightening.

Tietmeyer also said the governors had exchanged views on the situation in Asia and specifically Thailand, but did not say if they were especially concerned about the floating of the baht. "We have to monitor problems around the world," he said.
Thailand last week scrapped a tightly controlled exchange rate regime and allowed the overvalued baht to fall under a new managed-float system.
Economists expect Thailand's trade deficit to widen due to soaring import bills and inflation to rise due to the move.
Tietmeyer also said the G10 central bankers saw no problem with inflation in Europe despite a rise of import prices in some countries.

Global economic growth prospects were positive but structural unemployment remained Europe's biggest problem, he said, adding that central banks had done all they could with monetary policies to help to create jobs.

"On the one hand there is continued macroeconomic growth and this will continue according to expectations, but the problem is structural problems responsible for unemployment," Tietmeyer said. "It is not monetary policy that will solve these structural problems."
Some labour market reforms were already underway and needed to be continued to boost job creation, he said.
Although the G10 governors saw signs of some increase in real investment in Europe, it tended to boost productivity in existing sectors rather than create new business sectors, Tietmeyer said.
Tietmeyer also said the U.S. economy remained on a positive path, Britain and Canada were doing well and the central bankers believed there was now a chance for an economic pickup in Japan.
The G10 actually has 11 members -- the United States, Canada, Japan, Germany, France, Britain, Italy, the Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden and Switzerland.
